text: Two concepts decide where a row of data lives and who can see it: the business unit and the ledger. They sound similar, but they answer different questions. This lesson separates them cleanly, because almost every table in this course carries a column tied to one or the other.

A business unit is the operational boundary — which office or division a transaction belongs to. Nearly every transaction table carries a business unit I-D column for exactly this reason. It's also a security boundary: a clerk assigned to one business unit can't see or enter transactions stamped with another, no matter what they're looking at.

A ledger is a different boundary: the actual set of accounting books a journal entry posts into. Every ledger is defined by four things, nicknamed the four C's: chart of accounts, calendar, currency, and convention. Ledgers live in the GL_LEDGERS table, and a company can have a primary ledger plus optional secondary and reporting-currency ledgers tied back to it.

These two don't have to match one to one. Several business units can all post into the same ledger. But each business unit is always assigned one primary ledger for its transactions. So a transaction's business unit tells you operational ownership, while its journal entry's ledger I-D tells you which books it landed in. Related ideas, different questions.

Data access is layered on top of both, separately. Business units secure who can process subledger transactions. A separate data access set secures who can view or act on ledgers in General Ledger itself. A user might run GL reports across three ledgers but only enter invoices in one business unit — keep those two layers distinct.
